props.title: Danton
props.initialSlug: Revolutionary titan faces brutal political betrayal

sections.content: **Danton** (1983) stands as one of cinema's most gripping examinations of revolutionary idealism turned to terror. Andrzej Wajda's masterful direction pits Georges Danton (Gérard Depardieu) against Maximilien Robespierre (Wojciech Pszoniak) in a political death match that resonates with Poland's Solidarity movement of the 1980s. The film's claustrophobic interiors and rain-soaked streets of Paris create an atmosphere of paranoid tension similar to Costa-Gavras's **Z** (1969) and **State of Siege** (1972), while its exploration of power corruption recalls Pontecorvo's **The Battle of Algiers** (1966).

sections.content: The film's relevance extends beyond its historical setting, connecting to other powerful examinations of revolutionary idealism like **The Death of Stalin** (2017) and **Animal Farm** (1954). Wajda's direction emphasizes the personal toll of political upheaval, showing how former friends become mortal enemies when ideology hardens into dogma. The scenes between Danton and Robespierre crackle with theatrical intensity while maintaining documentary-like authenticity in their period detail.

What sets **Danton** apart is its unflinching look at the mechanics of political terror. Like **The Lost Honor of Katharina Blum** (1975) and **Missing** (1982), it shows how revolutionary justice becomes a mockery of legal proceedings. The trial scenes, with their predetermined outcomes and theatrical performances, mirror similar moments in **The Trial** (1962) and **In the Name of the Father** (1993). sections.content: Wajda's film connects to a broader tradition of revolutionary cinema, from Eisenstein's **October** (1928) to Bertolucci's **1900** (1976). The way it captures the gradual corruption of revolutionary ideals particularly resonates with films like **Land and Freedom** (1995) and **Reds** (1981). The attention to historical detail in costume and setting rivals that of **Barry Lyndon** (1975), while maintaining the political urgency of **The Conformist** (1970).
